Arrian's transmission is explained; Discourses uses George Long 1877, Enchiridion uses the version credited to Elizabeth Carter by MIT. The Handbook source budget includes Zeno's model-character selection.

George Long translation; five existing IDs retained and five new passages drawn from different books.

explorers-extra.scope: 40 citable selections for four explorers, ten each. Records distinguish surviving authorial words, later transmitted accounts and literary portrayals.
explorers-extra.method: Exact continuous excerpts inspected in the linked editions. No fabricated dialogue, motivational misattributions, artificially divided URLs, or isolated-word padding. All source-page budgets are at most 25 quoted words; Joaquin Miller’s poem is limited to nine words across its two selections as a conservative allowance for musical settings. Year can indicate composition, publication or the explicitly identified edition, as explained by locator/context.

entries.locator: Prologue; Fordham excerpt

sources.label: Journal of the First Voyage

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. An intention to record the voyage, preserved through the later journal tradition. Columbus’s original log is lost; the surviving text is not an autograph.

entries.locator: Prologue; Fordham excerpt

sources.label: Journal of the First Voyage

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. Columbus proposes repeated navigational trials and record keeping. The prologue also anticipates lost sleep; it is a historical description, not advice to neglect rest.

entries.locator: Description of islanders; King’s College London edition

sources.label: Letter to Luis de Santángel

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. Columbus describes Indigenous generosity in a self-promoting report. This praise coexists in the same letter with his admission that he seized people by force; it does not excuse conquest.

entries.locator: Description of Indigenous navigation; King’s College London edition

sources.label: Letter to Luis de Santángel

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. Recognition of the islanders’ navigational knowledge, amid a colonial report that also misrepresents and exploits them. The wording is the translation in the cited scholarly edition.

entries.locator: Opening; undated letter

sources.label: Letter concerning the colonisation and commerce of Española

entries.locator: Proposed regulation 6

sources.label: Letter concerning the colonisation and commerce of Española

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. Columbus proposes multiple witnesses for handling the crown’s gold. This is a financial-control proposal within a colonial extraction programme, not a claim that his rule was just.

entries.locator: Cecil Jane translation, vol. 2, p. 22

sources.label: Account of the Third Voyage

sources.label: Columbus

entries.locator: Stanza 1; Poems That Every Child Should Know

sources.label: Columbus

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. A nineteenth-century poetic portrayal of Columbus facing uncertainty. The poem’s heroic perspective is not a balanced history of the voyage or its consequences.

entries.locator: Attempt to recover Spanish captives; MacNutt translation

sources.label: First Letter of Relation

entries.locator: Description of Tenochtitlan’s marketplace; MacNutt translation

sources.label: Second Letter of Relation

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. Cortés describes food service in the Mexica capital. These are observations of Indigenous urban life, in a letter written to justify his conquest.

entries.subject: Hernán Cortés
entries.locator: Description of Tenochtitlan’s marketplace; MacNutt translation

sources.label: Second Letter of Relation

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. His report notices the organisation of a great Indigenous market. Its commercial sophistication belongs to the city he describes, not to the invading Spaniards.

entries.locator: The failed catapult during the siege; MacNutt translation

sources.label: Third Letter of Relation

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. An explicit admission that he concealed a failed weapon by claiming compassion. A lesson in reading a commander’s self-presentation critically, not an endorsement of deception.

entries.subject: Hernán Cortés

sources.label: Fourth Letter of Relation

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. Cortés uses this observation while explaining local artillery production. The immediate context is armed colonial control, rather than an innocent general maxim.

entries.subject: Hernán Cortés
entries.locator: Provisioning the Honduras expedition; MacNutt translation

sources.label: Fourth Letter of Relation

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. He says he bought provisions in Cuba to avoid demanding them from local people. This particular logistical claim does not cancel the coercion and enslavement described elsewhere in the letter.

entries.subject: Hernán Cortés
entries.locator: Journey towards Çagoatespan; MacNutt translation

sources.label: Fifth Letter of Relation

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. Lost in dense forest, Cortés combines a compass with the direction given by Indigenous guides. The account makes their local knowledge essential to the route.

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. He promises to investigate whether connecting waterways make Yucatán an island. The conjecture is not accepted geography; the useful point is the stated need to check it.

entries.locator: 2 April 1587; Folger, Elizabethan Court Day by Day, 1587, p. 18

sources.label: Letter to Francis Walsingham

entries.locator: 27 April 1587, postscript; Folger, Elizabethan Court Day by Day, 1587, p. 21

sources.label: Letter to John Wolley

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. After the raid on Cadiz, Drake pairs prayer with practical defensive preparation. This is a wartime letter, not a neutral maxim about present-day nations.

entries.locator: 21 July 1588; Folger, Elizabethan Court Day by Day, 1588, p. 30

sources.label: Letter to Lord Henry Seymour

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. Reporting the Armada’s arrival, Drake qualifies this judgement with 'as far as we perceive'. He recognises his opponents’ determination rather than dismissing them.

entries.locator: 31 July 1588; Folger, Elizabethan Court Day by Day, 1588, p. 33

sources.label: Letter to Francis Walsingham

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. Drake reports following Lord Admiral Howard’s instructions concerning Spanish prisoners. A documented glimpse of command responsibilities during the Armada campaign.

entries.locator: Dedicatory epistle, 1 January 1592 Old Style (1593); 1910 edition transcription

sources.label: Dedicatory epistle printed in Sir Francis Drake Revived

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. Drake’s dedicatory letter frames recording experience as a resource for those who follow. Dated 1 January 1592 in the old calendar, it was published after his death with the voyage account.

entries.locator: Planning with John Drake and the Cimaroons; voyage of 1572–1573

sources.label: Sir Francis Drake Revived

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. Nichols’s compiled report describes Drake consulting experienced companions before choosing his next move. This is a partisan expedition account assembled from participants’ reports, not Drake’s own wording.

entries.locator: California encounter, June 1579; National Humanities Center excerpt, p. 3

sources.label: The World Encompassed

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. The nephew’s compilation from Fletcher’s and other voyage notes describes Drake’s treatment of the Coastal Miwok. Its surrounding claims that Indigenous people worshipped Europeans are the visitors’ interpretation, not established Indigenous belief.

entries.subject: Francis Drake
entries.locator: Decision to cross the Pacific, July 1579; National Humanities Center excerpt, p. 6

sources.label: The World Encompassed

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. The voyage account describes Drake abandoning a northern passage after worsening cold and contrary winds, then turning towards the Moluccas with the company’s consent. The decision is reported by later compilers.

entries.subject: Francis Drake
entries.locator: Collected Poems edition, p. 275

sources.label: Drake

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. Noyes imagines Drake inviting Thomas Doughty below for wine during an uneasy conversation. It is hospitality inside a dramatic poem, not recorded historical dialogue.

entries.subject: Francis Drake
entries.locator: Collected Poems edition, p. 268

sources.label: Drake

entries.evidence: Exact continuous passage inspected in the cited edition. The poem imagines Drake choosing the western ocean if England falls to Spanish rule. This is Noyes’s romantic national portrayal, not Drake’s authenticated words or an account of Indigenous freedom.

exclusions.subject: Christopher Columbus
exclusions.reason: Original first-voyage log is lost; surviving prologue is transmitted, not an autograph. The letter to Ferdinand and Isabella has disputed dating, so c.1493–1494 is shown. Indigenous hospitality is credited to Indigenous people rather than portrayed as Columbus’s achievement. Miller is literature, not historical speech.

exclusions.subject: Hernán Cortés
exclusions.reason: The 1519 first letter is the Vera Cruz council’s account, not Cortés’s lost first letter. City services and markets belong to Indigenous civilisation. Deception, siege logistics and colonial motives are explained and withheld from daily rotation.

exclusions.subject: Leif Erikson
exclusions.reason: No surviving personal writings are claimed. Six medieval narrative selections are explicitly accounts and excluded from daily rotation; four are later novels labelled as portrayals. The Leif Ossurson in other Heimskringla chapters is a different person and was not used. A modern fictional Thorkyr saga found in search was excluded. The Greenlanders source is Eiður Eyþórsson’s 2024 direct translation; the two passages total 22 words.

exclusions.subject: Francis Drake
exclusions.reason: The modern 'Disturb us, Lord' prayer was excluded. The famous beginning/continuing aphorism was not added because the directly retrievable primary edition was unavailable. Armada bowls folklore was not used. Folger excerpts are cited to the exact dated letters; John Wolley’s letter is not mislabelled as a letter to Walsingham. The 1593 dedication’s Old Style date is explicit. Partisan voyage accounts and Noyes’s fiction are identified rather than passed off as Drake’s own testimony.
